procedural_history.originating_court: High Court of Judicature at Bombay
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 13.10.2015 in CRLAP No.88 of 2015, CONFC No.4 of 2014 and SC No.407 of 2010 and dated 14.10.2015 in CONFC No.4 of 2014 and CRLAP No.88 of 2015
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Judicature at Bombay issued a Judgment and Order in CRLAP No.88 of 2015, CONFC No.4 of 2014 and SC No.407 of 2010 on 13.10.2015 and in CONFC No.4 of 2014 and CRLAP No.88 of 2015 on 14.10.2015.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant preferred appeals to the Supreme Court challenging the High Court's Judgment and Order. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals and ordered the appellant to be set at liberty.

directions: The appellant be set at liberty forthwith, if not required in any other case.
Pending applications, if any, are also disposed of.

issue.issue_text: Whether non-recording of a disclosure statement of the appellant in the language in which it is made and recording of the same in a language totally unknown to the appellant, contents whereof are also not read over and explained to him, can be said to have caused any prejudice to the cause of justice?

facts: The appellant's vernacular language was Hindi.
The appellant gave a disclosure statement in Hindi.
The investigating officer recorded this statement in Marathi, a language the appellant did not know how to read or write.
The contents of the statement recorded in Marathi were not read over or explained to the appellant in Hindi.
law: An accused person must be able to understand the case of the prosecution against them.
Statutory safeguards related to language must be complied with during legal proceedings.

Citing the Constitution Bench in *Syed Qasim Razvi v. State of Hyderabad*, the Court affirmed that if an accused does not understand the language of the proceedings and is not provided with adequate interpretation, it can cause prejudice to their trial.
application: The Court found that the appellant's inability to understand the recorded disclosure statement due to the language barrier was a significant disadvantage.
This created uncertainty as to whether the statement recorded by the police accurately reflected what the appellant had actually said.
The Court determined that this failure to record the statement in the appellant's language, or at least explain it to him, constituted a non-compliance with statutory safeguards.
This non-compliance prejudiced the appellant's case because he could not understand a key piece of evidence being used against him.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the non-recording of the disclosure statement in the language in which it was made (Hindi) and recording it in a language unknown to the appellant (Marathi) without explaining the contents, caused prejudice to the cause of justice.

issue.issue_text: Whether the circumstances as identified and relied on by the prosecution indeed point to the guilt only of the appellant, closing out any and all other possibilities of any other person?

facts: The prosecution's case was based on circumstantial evidence, including the 'last seen theory' and the fact that the appellant was found near the scene of the crime.
However, the Court noted that no witness testified to seeing the appellant and the prosecutrix together at any point in time.
The appellant and the victim had no relationship, and he was not a visitor to her house.
law: The Court reiterated the settled law on circumstantial evidence: when a case relies on such evidence, it must form a complete chain that points singularly to the guilt of the accused, closing out the possibility of all other hypotheses.
application: The Court examined the circumstances presented by the prosecution and found "yawning gaps in the chain of circumstances".
Specifically, it determined that the 'last seen theory' did not apply because there was no evidence placing the appellant and the victim together.
The Court criticized the lower courts for having "presumptuously assumed the guilt of the appellant" without proper analysis.
It concluded that the prosecution had not made the necessary efforts to prove the appellant's guilt to the exclusion of anyone else.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the prosecution's argument, concluding that the chain of circumstantial evidence was far from complete and did not exclusively point to the appellant's guilt, leaving open the possibility that another person could have committed the crime.

issue.issue_text: as to whether, even if the recovery on the search conducted on 13.6.2010, 16.6.2010 and 17.6.2010 is believed to be so, either on the basis of information obtained from the police during investigation or as a consequence of statement made by the appellant or any other material obtained by the police during the course of investigation, the same stands linked to the appellant or not.

facts: Police conducted searches and recovered items on three separate dates: June 13, June 16, and June 17, 2010.
The first search on June 13 was of the appellant's very small room (8.5 ft x 6.5 ft) and was conducted without the appellant present.

The subsequent searches on June 16 and 17 were allegedly based on disclosure statements made by the appellant while in custody, leading to the recovery of more items from the same room and another location.
The prosecution argued that these recovered items, some of which contained DNA evidence, linked the appellant to the crime.
application: The Court found the prosecution's case on this issue to be unproven for two main reasons.

First, the Court found the recovery of items on June 16 to be highly improbable. It questioned how, if the police had "microscopically scanned" the tiny room during a thorough search on June 13, they could have missed items that were supposedly recovered from the same room just three days later.
Second, the Court stated that even if the recoveries were believed, the articles themselves did not sufficiently link the appellant to the crime.
The Court's skepticism was reinforced by numerous contradictions in the evidence regarding the searches:

A witness (PW 5) to the first search claimed to have seen a blood-stained nicker, but the official record states this item was only recovered during the second search on June 16, making that recovery "extremely doubtful."

There were conflicting accounts regarding the timing of the first search and the justification for it, with the victim's father stating he didn't suspect the appellant until a day after the search was conducted.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the recovered items linked the appellant to the crime. It concluded that the prosecution had failed to prove its case because the circumstances of the recoveries, particularly the second search on June 16, were highly doubtful, improbable, and riddled with contradictions, which undermined the credibility of the evidence.

arguments.issue_text: Whether non-recording of a disclosure statement of the appellant in the language in which it is made and recording of the same in a language totally unknown to the appellant, contents whereof are also not read over and explained to him, can be said to have caused any prejudice to the cause of justice?
appellant_arguments: The disclosure statements (Ext.47 & Ext.50) were recorded in Marathi, a language the appellant did not know.
The contents of the statements were not read over or explained to the appellant in his vernacular language.
This failure to comply with statutory safeguards regarding language caused prejudice, as the correctness of the recorded statements is uncertain.
respondent_arguments: The disclosure statements made by the appellant were valid and led to the recovery of incriminating articles (Ext.48 and Ext.51).

arguments.issue_text: Whether the circumstances as identified and relied on by the prosecution indeed point to the guilt only of the appellant, closing out any and all other possibilities of any other person?
appellant_arguments: The circumstances relied upon by the prosecution do not conclusively prove guilt, and the lower courts presumptuously assumed the appellant's guilt without proper consideration.
respondent_arguments: The circumstances, particularly the disclosure statements leading to the recovery of incriminating articles, form a complete chain of evidence pointing exclusively to the appellant's guilt.

arguments.issue_text: as to whether, even if the recovery on the search conducted on 13.6.2010, 16.6.2010 and 17.6.2010 is believed to be so, either on the basis of information obtained from the police during investigation or as a consequence of statement made by the appellant or any other material obtained by the police during the course of investigation, the same stands linked to the appellant or not.
appellant_arguments: The items recovered during the investigation are not sufficiently linked to the appellant or the crime.
respondent_arguments: The recovery of incriminating articles, such as clothes belonging to the appellant and the prosecutrix, was a direct consequence of the appellant's disclosure statements and therefore is directly linked to him.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When a case is governed by circumstantial evidence, the evidence must point singularly to the guilt of the appellant, closing out the possibility of all other hypotheses.
obiter: The necessity of compliance with Section 53A was observed.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The lower courts failed in their judicial duty by being swayed by the horrific and depraved nature of the crime, leading them to presumptuously assume the appellant's guilt without properly analyzing the evidence and considering all relevant aspects of the case.
legal_tests_applied: The implicit standard that courts must not be influenced by the heinous nature of an alleged crime when evaluating evidence, but must instead conduct a dispassionate and objective analysis.

The principle that in a case based on circumstantial evidence, the prosecution must establish a complete chain of evidence that points exclusively to the guilt of the accused, a standard the lower courts failed to apply by presumptuously assuming guilt.
policy_considerations: Investigating authorities have not only a legal, but also a moral duty to conduct fair and proper investigations and take all possible steps within the letter of the law to bring perpetrators of heinous crimes to justice.

The judiciary must guard against allowing the heart-breaking and horrific nature of a crime to prompt a confirmation of guilt and a severe sentence, as this can lead to a miscarriage of justice where the evidence is not properly scrutinized.
